questions.question: What does the Quranic concept of 'mukhlis lahu al-din' in verse 2 require of a believer?
options: A. Performing a minimum number of prayers each day without exception
B. Dedicating all acts of worship exclusively to Allah with no trace of showing off or mixed motives
C. Memorizing the Quran before undertaking any voluntary act of worship
D. Seeking the approval of scholars before performing supererogatory deeds
questions.explanation: Verse 2 commands worship of Allah 'mukhlisan lahu al-din,' meaning to make religion exclusively and purely for Allah, free from desire for people's praise or worldly motivation. Ibn Kathir explains that ikhlas here means al-tawhid — pure monotheism expressed through every act of worship — and that any worship contaminated by riya (showing off) constitutes a form of minor shirk.

questions.question: True or false: Imam al-Tabari explains that the word 'tanzil' in verse 1 emphasizes gradual, deliberate revelation rather than the Quran being delivered all at once.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari in his Jami al-Bayan explains that 'tanzil' (sending-down) emphasizes the gradual and deliberate manner of the Quran's revelation. He further notes that the participial noun tanzil rather than a past-tense verb carries the sense of revelation continuously descending upon and penetrating believing hearts.

questions.question: According to Ibn Kathir and Imam al-Tabari, what was the core justification the Meccan polytheists used for worshipping idols alongside Allah?
options: A. They believed the idols were equal to Allah in creative power
B. They claimed the idols were intermediaries who would bring them nearer to Allah
C. They thought the idols could independently grant provision and offspring
D. They argued that worshipping many gods brought a wider guarantee of protection
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir and Imam al-Tabari both explain that the Meccan polytheists did not deny Allah's supremacy. Their specific rationalization was 'ma na'buduhum illa liyuqarribuna ila Allahi zulfa' — we only worship them so they may bring us nearer to Allah. The verse quotes and then refutes this logic, declaring that Allah does not guide the persistent liar and ungrateful disbeliever.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 4 refutes the notion of divine offspring by first entertaining the hypothetical that Allah could have chosen from His creation, then immediately negating it through the declaration 'subhanahu' and the Names al-Wahid al-Qahhar.
questions.explanation: Verse 4 employs a conditional hypothetical — 'if He had intended' — not to suggest it is possible but as a rhetorical argument that collapses under examination. The verse responds with 'Exalted is He' (subhanahu) and affirms His Names al-Wahid (the Uniquely One) and al-Qahhar (the Subduer), which together negate any need for offspring, heir, or companion. Wahbah al-Zuhayli identifies this method as 'ilzam' — binding the opponent with their own logic.

questions.question: Which contemporary scholar argued that Islam's rejection of unauthorized intermediaries in worship represents a liberation of human consciousness from dependency on spiritual brokers?
options: A. Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir
B. Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran
C. Muhammad al-Sha'rawi in his Quranic commentaries
D. Ibn Uthaymeen in his doctrinal teachings
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran argues that the Quranic declaration that pure religion belongs to Allah alone establishes a direct, unmediated relationship between the individual soul and its Creator, freeing human beings from dependency on supposed spiritual brokers. He views this as not merely a theological correction but a revolutionary liberation of human consciousness.

questions.question: Verse 9 contrasts the sincere night worshipper with the heedless person, then poses a rhetorical question. What term does the verse use for those capable of truly grasping this distinction?
options: A. Al-muttaqun (the God-fearing)
B. Al-mukhlisun (the sincere ones)
C. Ahl al-albab (people of understanding)
D. Al-muqarrabun (those brought near)
questions.explanation: Verse 9 asks 'Are those who know equal to those who do not know?' and identifies only 'ahl al-albab' — people of sound intellect and heart — as those who truly reflect on this distinction. Imam al-Qurtubi explains that these are people whose hearts have been refined by reflection, combining intellectual clarity with moral commitment to act upon what they know.

questions.question: True or false: Sayyid Qutb describes the image of the night worshipper in verse 9 as one of the most sublime images of human dignity in the entire Quran, because this person is driven by internal reality rather than social expectation.
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran describes the person who rises from sleep to stand and prostrate alone in the darkness as embodying 'one of the most sublime images of human dignity in the entire Quran.' He emphasizes that this worshipper is not constrained by social expectation or public display but driven entirely by genuine, internalized awareness of Allah and the Hereafter.

questions.question: What unique reward does verse 10 of Az-Zumar promise specifically and only to the patient?
options: A. Entry into Paradise without any questioning on the Day of Judgment
B. Their reward will be given 'bi-ghayri hisab' — without account or measure
C. They will be raised in the company of the prophets and the truthful
D. They will be spared any trial in the grave
questions.explanation: Verse 10 closes with 'innama yuwaffa al-sabirun ajrahum bi-ghayri hisab' — the patient will be given their reward without account. Imam al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb explains that this reward transcends the arithmetic of deeds and enters the realm of pure divine generosity. Wahbah al-Zuhayli notes this 'without account' is unique in the Quran and applies exclusively to the quality of sabr.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir notes that some early scholars connected the glad tidings of verse 17 specifically to pre-Islamic monotheists such as Zayd bin Amr bin Nufayl, while affirming that the verse is ultimately universal in scope.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir records that some early scholars held verse 17 was revealed concerning figures like Zayd bin Amr bin Nufayl, Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, and Salman al-Farisi — men who had turned away from idol worship before Islam's formal proclamation. Ibn Kathir then affirms the correct scholarly position that the verse applies universally to all who abandon shirk and sincerely embrace tawhid.

questions.question: What does Wahbah al-Zuhayli observe about the principle of 'following the best of speech' in verse 18 and its implication for Islamic scholarship?
options: A. Muslims should engage only with scholarship from their own school of jurisprudence
B. The verse endorses engaging with knowledge across disciplines while maintaining fidelity to Quranic principles
C. Believers should restrict their study to classical tafsir and avoid all contemporary commentary
D. The verse requires non-specialists to defer entirely to jurists without any independent reflection
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir observes that verse 18 affirms that the Muslim tradition at its best has always engaged with knowledge across disciplines while maintaining fidelity to Quranic principles. The capacity to listen discerningly and choose the best — modeled by the 'ahl al-albab' — represents intellectual engagement and openness rather than isolation.

questions.question: Verse 42 states that Allah takes souls at two distinct moments. What are those two moments, making sleep a form of 'lesser death'?
options: A. At birth and at the age of moral accountability
B. At the time of death and at the time of sleep
C. At the moment of major sin and at the moment of sincere repentance
D. At sunset each evening and at the moment of the final breath
questions.explanation: Verse 42 declares that Allah takes souls at the time of death (the greater death) and at the time of sleep (the lesser death). During sleep the soul is temporarily withheld and returned upon waking; for those whose appointed time has arrived, Allah retains it permanently. Ibn Abbas is reported by Ibn Kathir as saying: 'He keeps the souls of the dead and sends back the souls of the living, and He does not make any mistakes.'

questions.question: True or false: Muhammad al-Sha'rawi emphasized that verse 42's pairing of sleep and death reveals that life itself is a loan from Allah, returned each night and graciously given back each dawn.
questions.explanation: Muhammad al-Sha'rawi is cited in the contemporary commentary as emphasizing exactly this: verse 42's pairing of death and sleep reveals that life is a loan from Allah, returned each night and graciously given back each morning. This framing transforms the daily act of waking into a renewed expression of gratitude and absolute dependence on the Creator.

questions.question: Which senior Companion of the Prophet reportedly declared that verse 53 of Az-Zumar is the most hope-giving verse in the entire Quran?
options: A. Abu Hurayra
B. Anas ibn Malik
C. Abdullah ibn Masud
D. Umar ibn al-Khattab
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir records in his Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim that Abdullah ibn Masud declared verse 53 to be the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, with other Companions including Abdullah ibn Umar endorsing the same view. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith of the man who killed one hundred people as a narrative illustration that even the gravest sinner is not beyond Allah's mercy if they sincerely repent.

questions.question: True or false: The direct address 'O My servants' in verse 53 — spoken by Allah Himself to those who have sinned greatly — is understood by scholars to convey divine intimacy and care, showing that sin does not sever the bond with Allah as long as repentance remains available.
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that 'ya ibadi' (O My servants) is Allah directly claiming sinners as His own despite their transgressions, conveying an intimacy meant to draw them back. Imam al-Tabari affirms that this divine address shows the bond between Allah and the servant remains intact so long as the servant does not cut it through persistent refusal to repent.

questions.question: Ibn Uthaymeen describes verses 53 through 55 as a complete Quranic treatment of repentance. How does verse 54 function within this three-verse structure?
options: A. It limits the forgiveness of verse 53 to sins committed before puberty
B. It provides the practical action — repentance and submission — that must accompany the hope offered in verse 53
C. It cancels the promise of verse 53 for anyone who has ever committed shirk
D. It shifts the focus to collective community repentance rather than individual tawbah
questions.explanation: Ibn Uthaymeen describes the structure as: verse 53 opens the door with divine mercy, verse 54 requires the practical actions of repentance and submission, and verse 55 provides the ongoing program of following revelation. Wahbah al-Zuhayli similarly frames verse 54 as the practical complement to verse 53 — mercy is vast but must be seized through genuine turning to Allah before punishment arrives.

questions.question: What two failures will the condemned soul confess in the words recorded in verse 56 on the Day of Resurrection?
options: A. Neglecting the five daily prayers and failing to pay zakat
B. Neglecting duties toward Allah ('tafriti fi janbi Allah') and having been among those who mocked the truth
C. Disobeying parents and breaking ties of kinship
D. Failing to perform Hajj and abandoning the fast of Ramadan
questions.explanation: Verse 56 describes the soul crying 'Ya hasrata' (Alas, my regret) over two failures: 'tafriti fi janbi Allah' — neglecting what was owed to Allah — and the admission 'I was indeed among those who mocked.' Ibn Kathir notes this double failure compounds the tragedy: the person not only failed to do good but actively ridiculed those who did, closing off all internal correction.

questions.question: True or false: According to Ibn Kathir, the gates of Paradise in verse 73 are described as already open when the believers arrive — contrasting with Hell's gates — as a mark of divine honor and eager welcome prepared for the God-fearing.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir records that the gates of Paradise are opened before the believers arrive as a mark of honor and hospitality, in contrast to the gates of Hell. He also connects the plural 'gates' to the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim describing eight gates of Paradise, each associated with a different type of righteous deed, so that those who excelled in a particular virtue will be called from the corresponding gate.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb and Imam al-Tabari both note a profound literary connection between the closing words of verse 75 and the opening of the Quran. What is that connection?
options: A. Verse 75 uses the same Arabic root as the Basmalah, linking the end of judgment to the invocation of mercy
B. The phrase 'al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin' mirrors the opening of Surah Al-Fatiha, framing all of human history between the same expression of divine praise
C. Verse 75 repeats the exact words of verse 1 of Az-Zumar, forming an internal ring structure within the surah
D. The final verse of Az-Zumar echoes the last verse of Surah al-Baqarah, signaling the completion of revealed law
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari and Sayyid Qutb both observe that 'Alhamdulillahi Rabb al-Alamin' opens Surah Al-Fatiha — recited in every prayer — and closes the Day of Judgment scene in Az-Zumar. Qutb reflects that all of human history, from creation to resurrection to final judgment, is bookended by the same expression of divine praise, forming a grand thematic circle across the Quran.
